opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we get a lot. The short answer is that abundance isn't the same as usefulness. YouTube has an enormous amount of video, but most of it is third-person, edited, cut between camera angles, and filmed for an audience rather than for capturing how a task actually gets done. If you're a robot trying to learn manipulation, what you really need is the embodied perspective: where the hands are relative to the objects, how the head and eyes move to gather information before acting, the fine-grained contact and timing. That's very hard to recover from a cooking video shot from across the kitchen.

First-person, or egocentric, video is much closer to the robot's own sensory setup. A robot has cameras on its head or wrist, so the viewpoint gap is much smaller. And when we collect the data ourselves, with something like a head-mounted camera or smart glasses, we can also record the signals that matter: 3D hand poses, head motion, sometimes depth, all calibrated and synchronized. That turns passive video into something close to action-labeled demonstration data, which is what policy learning really wants.

The other piece is scalability in a different sense. Teleoperation is the gold standard for robot data, but it's slow and expensive and needs a robot in the loop. Egocentric human data sits in a sweet spot: it's far cheaper and more natural to collect than teleop, people can just go about their daily tasks, but it's far more structured and transferable than random internet video. So I don't see it as either-or. Internet video is great for broad priors, like semantics and what tasks look like. But for actually learning how to act, I think human-centric, first-person data is the more direct path, and it's a way to scale robot learning without being bottlenecked by the number of robots in the world.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts abundant YouTube video with the more useful, structured signals in first-person data, and compares both with costly teleoperation.

r002.rationale: It says first-person data narrows the viewpoint gap and is more transferable, but does not clearly state that human demonstrations need a distribution closely matched to robot data.

r003.rationale: It describes limitations of YouTube videos but does not identify finding the subset whose distribution aligns with robot data as a major difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I get a lot, because on the surface it does seem a little backwards. There's this enormous pile of human video out there, people cooking, assembling furniture, fixing bikes, and the obvious instinct is, let's just learn from all of that. And I'm not against that at all. I think it's going to be part of the picture. But when you actually sit down and try to turn a third-person YouTube clip into something a robot can act on, you run into a few problems that are pretty fundamental.

The first one is viewpoint. A robot, at least the kind we care about, is embodied. It sees the world from its own cameras, often mounted on the head or near the gripper, and it has to make decisions from that perspective. Third-person video is shot from wherever a human with a phone happened to be standing. So there's a huge gap between what the data looks like and what the robot will actually observe at deployment time. You can try to close that gap with clever representation learning, and people are doing good work there, but you're spending a lot of effort fighting the format of the data.

The second thing, and honestly this is the bigger one for me, is that third-person video mostly tells you what happened, not how it was done. You see a hand reach into a drawer and come out with a spoon. You don't really see the contact, the small adjustments, the moment the fingers close. All of the stuff that makes manipulation hard is happening in a few pixels, often occluded by the arm itself. Egocentric video, first-person video, puts the camera right where the action is. The hands are large in the frame, you see the object up close, you see the correction when something slips. That's the signal we actually need.

And the third piece is that when we collect first-person data ourselves, we get to control what else comes with it. We can attach hand pose, sometimes gaze, we know the task, we know the timing. With YouTube you get pixels and maybe a caption, and you're reverse-engineering everything else. So it's not that first-person is more plentiful, it's clearly not. It's that a smaller amount of data that's aligned with the robot's perspective and rich in the details of manipulation often gets you further than a huge amount of data you have to squint at.

The way I think about it is, YouTube is great for learning what the world looks like and what tasks exist, kind of the semantic layer. First-person data is where you learn how to actually do things with your hands. And ultimately I want both, but I'd rather start from the data that's closest to what the robot will experience.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts YouTube’s abundance with smaller first-person datasets that provide more useful, robot-relevant manipulation detail.

r002.rationale: It says third-person video has a large viewpoint gap from what the robot observes at deployment, and favors data closest to the robot’s experience.

r003.rationale: It describes YouTube’s viewpoint and detail problems, but does not identify finding the subset of YouTube videos whose distribution aligns with robot data as a major difficulty.

astra-6.text:
The key is that having a lot of video isn’t quite the same as having the right data for a robot to learn from. Third-person video can show you what a person is doing, but the camera might be across the room, the hands might be occluded, or the video might cut right at the moment of interaction. It’s harder to infer how the action actually happened.

With first-person video, you’re looking more directly at the objects and the hands interacting with them. That gives you a closer connection between what the agent sees and what it does, which is useful because a robot also has to choose actions based on its own observations.

It doesn’t solve everything—human hands and robot grippers are different, and video alone doesn’t tell you the forces involved. But it gives us a more useful starting point for learning manipulation. I see third-person video as complementary: it can provide broad knowledge about tasks, while first-person video gives us a better view of the interactions needed to carry them out.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the abundance of third-person video with whether it provides the right, useful learning signal for robots.

r002.rationale: It notes differences between human hands and robot grippers, but does not state that human demonstrations need a distribution closely matched to robot data.

r003.rationale: It discusses shortcomings of third-person video, but does not identify finding YouTube videos whose distribution aligns with robot data as a major difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
The abundance of video is really exciting, but for robot learning, the question is what you can learn from it. In a third-person YouTube video, you might see someone cooking, but the camera may be far away, their hands may be occluded, and the video may cut right at the moment of interaction. You can learn what the task looks like without necessarily learning how to do it.

First-person video gives you a much closer view of the relationship between the hands, the objects, and the environment. What did the person reach for? How did they approach it? What changed after they touched it? Those details are useful if you want to connect visual observations to actions.

It’s still not robot action data—you don’t automatically get forces or motor commands from a video. But it provides a better starting point for learning manipulation, and potentially a more scalable way to capture everyday interactions. I see third-person and first-person video as complementary: one gives you broad coverage, and the other gives you a closer view of the interaction.

r001.rationale: It contrasts first-person video’s closer, more useful interaction details with its potential to scale, while noting third-person video’s broader coverage.

r002.rationale: It says first-person video is a better starting point, but does not state that human demonstrations need a distribution closely matched to robot data.

r003.rationale: It does not identify selecting YouTube videos whose distribution aligns with robot data as a major difficulty.
